title: Email Delivery: SMTP, SPF, DKIM and DMARC
objectives: Trace how a message moves between mail servers with SMTP and MX records
Explain what SPF, DKIM and DMARC each check, and why alignment matters
Roll out a DMARC policy without losing legitimate mail

cards.title: How a message hops between mail servers
cards.body: An app hands mail to its provider’s submission server, usually on port 587 with authentication. That server looks up the recipient domain’s MX records and connects to the listed mail server on port 25. The receiver answers each step with a code: 2xx accepts, 5xx rejects permanently and the sender bounces the message, 4xx means try later. RFC 5321 asks senders to wait at least 30 minutes between retries and to keep trying for at least four to five days.

cards.title: Three checks a receiver runs
cards.body: SPF and DKIM authenticate domains; DMARC ties them to the From address people see.
steps: SPF: is the connecting IP allowed by the SPF record of the envelope sender’s domain (MAIL FROM)?
DKIM: does the signature verify with the public key at selector._domainkey of the signing domain d=?
DMARC: did SPF or DKIM pass for a domain that aligns with the visible From domain?
If not, apply the From domain’s policy: none, quarantine or reject
Send aggregate reports to the address the domain published, so its owner sees failures

cards.title: Worked example: SPF passes but DMARC fails
cards.body: Passing checks for the wrong domain does not satisfy DMARC.
steps: A shop sends From: billing@shop.example through an email provider
Envelope sender is bounces@mail.provider.example: SPF passes, for provider.example
DKIM signature has d=provider.example: DKIM passes, for provider.example
Neither domain aligns with shop.example, so DMARC fails; with p=reject the mail is refused
cards.note: Result. Two passing checks still fail DMARC. The fix is to sign with d=shop.example using a key the shop publishes, and to use a return-path such as bounce.shop.example, which aligns under the default relaxed rules.

cards.title: SPF stops at ten lookups
cards.body: RFC 7208 limits the mechanisms that cost DNS queries, such as include, a, mx and redirect, to 10 per check. Each provider’s include can contain more includes, and once the count passes 10, SPF returns a permanent error, which DMARC treats as a fail. SPF also breaks when mail is forwarded, because the forwarder’s IP is not in the original domain’s record. A DKIM signature travels with the message and survives forwarding unless the content changes, which is why DMARC needs only one of the two to pass and align.

cards.title: Trap: jumping straight to p=reject
cards.body: Companies send mail from many places: the app, a support desk, a marketing tool, payroll. Publishing p=reject first silently drops every sender that is not yet aligned. Start with p=none and a reporting address, read the aggregate reports for a few weeks, fix each legitimate sender, then move to quarantine and finally reject. DMARC is now specified in RFC 9989 (2026), which replaced RFC 7489.

questions.prompt: How does a sending mail server find where to deliver mail for someone@example.org?

choices.label: It looks up the MX records for example.org
It posts the message to example.org’s web server on port 443
It reads the delivery address from example.org’s SPF record
It asks the recipient’s ISP for a route over BGP

questions.explanation: MX records name the mail servers for a domain. Web servers do not accept mail; SPF lists who may send for a domain, not where to deliver; and BGP routes packets, not messages.

questions.prompt: A receiving server answers a delivery attempt with code 451. What should the sender do?

choices.label: Bounce the message to its author at once
Resend it in a tight loop until accepted
Queue it and retry later, for days if needed
Drop it, since 4xx means the address is wrong

questions.explanation: A 4xx reply is temporary, so the sender queues and retries with growing gaps. Bouncing is for 5xx; tight loops look like abuse and get blocked; and a wrong address returns a 5xx.

questions.prompt: SPF passes for mail.provider.example, DKIM passes with d=provider.example, and the visible From is shop.example. What does DMARC conclude?

choices.label: Pass, since both SPF and DKIM passed
Fail, since neither passing domain aligns with shop.example
Pass, as long as the provider’s IPs are listed in the SPF record
Neutral, since DMARC looks only at DKIM

questions.explanation: DMARC needs a pass for a domain matching the From domain. Both passes are for provider.example; listing IPs does not change which domain passed; and DMARC uses both SPF and DKIM.

questions.prompt: An SPF record includes six providers that together need 13 DNS lookups. What happens?

choices.label: Receivers evaluate the first 10 and accept the rest
Caching makes the lookup limit not apply
SPF passes, but with a lower spam score
Evaluation hits a permanent error and SPF fails

questions.explanation: Past 10 lookups RFC 7208 requires a permanent error. Receivers do not skip ahead; caching does not change the count; and a permerror is not a pass.

questions.prompt: Why does DKIM often survive mail forwarding when SPF does not?

choices.label: The signature travels with the message, but SPF checks the forwarder’s IP
Forwarders sign each message again using the original sending domain’s key
Receivers turn off SPF checks for forwarded mail
DKIM checks the recipient’s domain rather than the sender’s

questions.explanation: DKIM verifies content plus the signing domain’s key, wherever the message came from. Forwarders do not hold the original private key; receivers still run SPF; and DKIM verifies the signing domain, not the recipient.

questions.prompt: Order a safe DMARC rollout.

items.label: Read aggregate reports and fix unaligned senders
Publish SPF and DKIM for every sending service
Move the policy to reject
Publish DMARC with p=none and a reporting address
Move the policy to quarantine

questions.explanation: Authenticate, observe, fix, then tighten in steps so no legitimate sender is lost.

questions.prompt: An SPF record has include:a.example (which itself holds 2 includes), include:b.example (which holds 3), plus mx and a. How many DNS lookups count toward the limit?
assumptions: Each include, mx and a costs one lookup
Nested includes count too
The nested includes contain no further lookups
questions.explanation: Sanity check: nine of ten leaves room for just one more lookup, so adding another provider’s include could tip SPF into a permanent error.

flashcards.back: Whether the sending IP is allowed by the envelope sender domain’s record; at most 10 lookups.
A signature over the message, verified with the signing domain’s public key in DNS.
Alignment: SPF or DKIM must pass for the visible From domain, plus a policy and reports.

sources.title: RFC 9989: Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC)

mechanism.title: What happens between “send” and the inbox
steps: An application submits a message to a mail server it is allowed to use, authenticating on the submission port. The message has two sets of addresses: the envelope, used by SMTP for routing and bounces (MAIL FROM and RCPT TO), and the headers people see, including From. They often differ, for example when a provider handles bounces on its own domain.

The sending server resolves the recipient domain’s MX records, picks the lowest preference value first, and opens an SMTP session. The receiver can reject at any step with a 5xx code or defer with a 4xx. Deferred mail stays in the sender’s queue and is retried with backoff, so a temporary problem at the receiver delays mail by minutes or hours rather than losing it.

The receiver then authenticates. SPF looks up a TXT record on the envelope sender’s domain and asks whether the connecting IP is listed, directly or through includes. DKIM finds a signature header, fetches the public key at the selector the header names, and verifies a hash over the body and chosen headers. Each produces a result for a specific domain, which may not be the one in From.

DMARC closes that gap. It looks up a policy record at _dmarc on the From domain and requires that SPF or DKIM pass for an aligned domain: the same organisational domain under relaxed alignment, or the exact domain under strict alignment. If neither aligns, the receiver applies the policy, none, quarantine or reject, though it may still use its own judgement.

DMARC also asks receivers to send aggregate reports: daily XML summaries of which IPs sent mail claiming the domain and how they fared. These reports are how a domain owner finds forgotten senders before tightening the policy, and how it spots spoofing. Transport security is separate: STARTTLS is opportunistic by default, and MTA-STS lets a domain require TLS for mail sent to it.

useWhen: Any product that sends password resets, receipts or notifications from its own domain.
Protecting a brand domain from being spoofed in phishing.
avoidWhen: Avoid publishing p=reject before reports show every legitimate sender aligned.
Avoid stacking provider includes until SPF passes 10 lookups.

rows: Sending IP is authorised for the envelope domain
Mail is forwarded; more than 10 lookups
Signature from the signing domain’s key
A list or gateway modifies the signed content
An aligned SPF or DKIM pass for the From domain
Senders pass only for their own domain

numbers.title: Counting an SPF record
assumptions: include:a.example holding 2 more includes
include:b.example holding 3 more includes
mx and a mechanisms on the domain itself
steps: Provider A: 1 lookup for the include plus 2 nested = 3.
Provider B: 1 plus 3 nested = 4.
The mx and a mechanisms: 1 each = 2.
Total 3 + 4 + 2 = 9 of the 10 allowed; one more provider include with any nesting tips it over.
numbers.result: The record works today but is one vendor away from a permanent error, so flatten it or move a sender to its own subdomain.

india.title: SMTP, SPF, DKIM and DMARC in the RFCs
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 5321 defines SMTP, MX-based delivery and the retry guidance of at least 30 minutes between attempts and four to five days before giving up. RFC 7208 defines SPF and its 10-lookup limit. RFC 6376 defines DKIM signatures and key lookup. RFC 9989, published in May 2026, is the standards-track DMARC specification that replaced RFC 7489, with RFC 9990 and RFC 9991 covering aggregate and failure reports.

pitfalls.trap: “SPF and DKIM both pass, so DMARC is fine.”
pitfalls.say: “They have to pass for a domain aligned with From; passing for the provider’s domain still fails DMARC.”
“I’d start at p=none, read the reports, fix each sender, then tighten.”

takeaways: Mail routes by MX records; 4xx means retry later, 5xx means bounce.
SPF authorises sending IPs and allows at most 10 DNS lookups.
DKIM signs the message and survives forwarding unless content changes.
DMARC needs an aligned pass for the From domain; roll out from p=none.

interactive.title: Where did the password resets go?
interactive.prompt: Yesterday you changed your domain’s DMARC policy from none to reject. Today support says password-reset mails sent by your helpdesk vendor are not arriving. Your app’s own mail still arrives. What happened?

choices.label: A reject policy blocks every automated sender
choices.feedback: DMARC does not care whether mail is automated; your app’s mail still arrives because it is aligned.

choices.label: DMARC records take about a week to take effect
choices.feedback: A DMARC record is a DNS TXT record; it takes effect as caches expire, typically within hours.

choices.label: The vendor sends as your domain without aligned SPF or DKIM
choices.feedback: Right: the vendor’s mail passes only for its own domain, so DMARC fails and receivers now reject it.

interactive.reveal: Every service that sends as your domain needs aligned SPF or DKIM, usually by adding a DKIM key the vendor provides under your domain. Aggregate reports under p=none would have shown this sender failing before the switch.

seeAlso.why: MX, TXT and the DNS lookups every mail check depends on
Idempotent sends keep mail retries from producing duplicates
How resolvers cache the records SPF, DKIM and DMARC fetch

title: DDoS: Floods, Amplification and Absorption
objectives: Tell apart volumetric, protocol and application-layer floods
Explain SYN floods, SYN cookies and reflection amplification
Decide where each kind of attack must be absorbed or filtered

cards.title: Three ways to exhaust a service
cards.body: A volumetric attack fills the pipes, measured in Gbit/s, so nothing behind the link matters. A protocol attack exhausts state in servers or middleboxes, such as half-open TCP connections or a firewall’s connection table. An application-layer attack sends valid-looking requests that are expensive to serve, such as searches or logins, measured in requests per second. Each needs a defence in a different place.

cards.title: How a SYN flood fills the queue, and how SYN cookies empty it
cards.body: The attacker sends SYNs but never completes the handshake.
steps: The attacker sends SYNs with forged source addresses
The server stores a half-open entry and sends SYN-ACKs to the forged addresses
Entries wait for an ACK that never comes, through several SYN-ACK retries
The half-open queue fills and real clients’ SYNs are dropped
With SYN cookies the server encodes the connection details in its sequence number, stores nothing, and rebuilds the entry from a valid ACK

cards.title: Worked example: sizing a reflection attack
cards.body: Reflection sends a small spoofed request to a server that sends a large reply to the victim.
steps: Assume: a 64-byte query with the victim’s address as source triggers a 3,200-byte answer
Amplification factor: 3,200 ÷ 64 = 50
Attackers send 1 Gbit/s of spoofed queries to many open servers
The victim receives 1 × 50 = 50 Gbit/s of answers
Against a 10 Gbit/s uplink, that is five times the capacity
cards.note: Result. In this illustrative case the link is full before any packet reaches a server, so nothing on the server can help. The flood must be absorbed by networks with more capacity than the attack.

cards.title: Absorb at the edge, before your link
cards.body: Volumetric floods are absorbed upstream: anycast spreads them over many sites, and scrubbing services filter at a scale no single site has. Hide the origin by accepting traffic only from the CDN or proxy in front of it. Providers that apply source-address validation (BCP 38) stop their customers from sending spoofed packets, which removes reflection at its root. Application floods are handled closer in: caching, rate limits per client or key, and challenges for suspicious traffic.

cards.title: Trap: blocking the attacking addresses
cards.body: In a SYN flood the source addresses are forged; in a reflection attack they belong to innocent open servers; in an application flood they may be tens of thousands of home devices. Blocking addresses one by one cannot keep up and can block real users. Filter by what the traffic is instead: drop unexpected UDP from ports 53, 123 or 11211 at the edge of a web service, rate-limit expensive endpoints, and challenge clients that look automated.

questions.prompt: During a SYN flood, real users cannot connect though the server’s CPU is mostly idle. Why?

choices.label: Half-open entries fill the queue, so new SYNs are dropped
The server has run out of TLS session keys for new clients
The attack has taken every port on the server
Forged packets have corrupted the routing table

questions.explanation: The limit is the half-open queue, not CPU. TLS has not started for half-open connections; a server port serves many connections, so ports are not used up; and forged sources do not alter routes.

questions.prompt: What do SYN cookies change?

choices.label: Clients must solve a puzzle before sending a SYN
The server holds no state until the client’s ACK returns
The server attaches a browser cookie to its SYN-ACK
A firewall blocks addresses that send many SYNs

questions.explanation: The connection details ride in the server’s initial sequence number, so forged SYNs cost no memory. There is no client puzzle in TCP; browser cookies are an HTTP feature; and source blocking is a separate, weaker defence.

questions.prompt: Why do reflection attacks use UDP services such as DNS rather than TCP ones?

choices.label: UDP packets are always larger than TCP packets
TCP services cannot be reached from the internet
With no handshake, a forged source gets the full reply
DNS servers keep no log of who sent which query to them

questions.explanation: TCP would send only a SYN-ACK to the forged address and stop, while UDP answers at once in full. Packet size depends on content, not the protocol; TCP services are reachable; and logging does not decide what gets reflected.

questions.prompt: A 300 Gbit/s flood targets a site with a 10 Gbit/s uplink. Where must it be stopped?

choices.label: In the application’s request handlers
Upstream, in networks bigger than the flood
With firewall rules on each web server
By autoscaling web servers behind the uplink

questions.explanation: Once the uplink is full, everything behind it starves. Handlers, host firewalls and extra servers all sit behind the saturated link.

questions.prompt: Valid HTTPS search requests from 50,000 home IP addresses overload the database. What fits best?

choices.label: Block each attacking address by hand
Turn on SYN cookies on the web servers
Raise the uplink from 10 to 40 Gbit/s
Cache and rate-limit searches, and challenge bots

questions.explanation: The cost is per request, so reduce the work per request and the number of requests per client. Hand-blocking cannot keep up; the handshakes complete, so SYN cookies do nothing; and the link is not the bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of a SYN flood without SYN cookies.

items.label: The half-open queue fills
The server stores half-open entries
Real clients’ SYNs are dropped
SYN-ACKs go to forged addresses and get no reply
Forged SYNs arrive

questions.explanation: Each forged SYN costs an entry until it times out, so the queue fills and real users are turned away.

questions.prompt: A 64-byte spoofed query triggers a 3,200-byte reply. Attackers send 1 Gbit/s of such queries. How many Gbit/s reach the victim?
assumptions: Every query is answered
Replies all go to the victim
questions.explanation: Design implication: 50 Gbit/s is more than most single sites can take in, so defence has to live upstream, not on the servers.

flashcards.back: Volumetric (fills links), protocol (exhausts state), application (expensive requests).
The server stores nothing for a SYN; it rebuilds state from the returning ACK.
Reply size ÷ request size; the victim gets attack rate × factor.

sources.title: RFC 4987: TCP SYN Flooding Attacks and Common Mitigations
AWS: Best Practices for DDoS Resiliency

mechanism.title: Where each flood bites and where it is stopped
steps: Every service has a narrowest point: link capacity, a table of connection state, or the work per request. A denial-of-service attack aims at one of them. Distributed attacks use many sources, from botnets of compromised devices to reflection through innocent servers, so they cannot be stopped by blocking one sender.

A SYN flood targets the TCP handshake. For each SYN, a server normally allocates an entry, sends a SYN-ACK and waits, resending a few times. Forged SYNs never complete, so entries pile up until the queue is full and real SYNs are dropped. SYN cookies, described in RFC 4987, let the server skip the entry: it encodes the connection details and a secret-keyed hash into its initial sequence number, and rebuilds them when a valid ACK returns.

Reflection attacks forge the victim’s address as the source of small UDP queries to servers that answer with much larger replies: open DNS resolvers, time servers or misconfigured caches. The victim receives the replies from thousands of legitimate-looking servers. The amplification factor, reply size divided by request size, multiplies the attacker’s bandwidth, and spoofing is possible only where networks do not apply ingress filtering as BCP 38 recommends.

Volumetric attacks must be absorbed where capacity exceeds the flood. Anycast announces the service from many sites so the flood splits among them, and providers’ scrubbing centres drop attack traffic by protocol, port and pattern before forwarding clean traffic. The origin should accept traffic only from the edge, so attackers cannot bypass it by aiming straight at the origin’s address.

Application-layer floods look like real users and arrive over completed connections, so network filters cannot tell them apart. Defences work per request: cache expensive responses, rate-limit by client, account or key, require challenges for suspicious clients, and shed load before the database falls over. Autoscaling helps briefly but turns an attack into a large bill if no limit is set.

useWhen: Any public service, since a modest flood can fill a small site’s link.
Designing an origin behind a CDN, load balancer or scrubbing service.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on per-address blocking against forged or widely distributed sources.
Avoid unlimited autoscaling as the only defence against request floods.

rows: SYN cookies, larger queues, edge proxies
Caching, rate limits, challenges, load shedding

numbers.title: Can the uplink survive a reflection attack?
assumptions: 64-byte spoofed query, 3,200-byte reply
Attackers send 1 Gbit/s of queries
The site has a 10 Gbit/s uplink
steps: Amplification: 3,200 ÷ 64 = 50.
Arriving at the victim: 1 Gbit/s × 50 = 50 Gbit/s.
Uplink headroom: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 times over capacity.
Even with filters on the servers, 40 Gbit/s of the flood is dropped at random before reaching them, real traffic included.
numbers.result: The site cannot defend itself behind its own uplink; the attack must be absorbed upstream by an edge or scrubbing provider.

india.title: SYN flooding and ingress filtering in the RFCs, and AWS guidance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 4987 surveys SYN flooding attacks and mitigations, including SYN caches and SYN cookies, and explains their trade-offs. RFC 2827, also known as BCP 38, asks network operators to drop packets whose source addresses could not have come from the customer network that sent them, which blocks spoofing and therefore reflection. The AWS whitepaper on DDoS resiliency recommends reducing the attack surface, absorbing volumetric attacks at edge locations and scaling to absorb application-layer floods while protecting the origin.

pitfalls.say: “The sources are forged or innocent reflectors, so I’d filter by protocol and absorb upstream instead.”
“It helps with request floods for a while, but a volumetric attack fills the link first, and unlimited scaling becomes a bill.”

takeaways: Volumetric floods fill links, protocol floods exhaust state, application floods exhaust work.
SYN cookies let a server keep no state until the handshake completes.
Amplification = reply size ÷ request size; spoofing makes reflection possible.
Absorb floods upstream and let the origin accept traffic only from the edge.

interactive.title: Attackers found your origin
interactive.prompt: Your site sits behind a CDN, but a flood now hits the origin servers’ public address directly, bypassing the CDN. What do you do first?

choices.label: Add more origin servers to absorb the traffic
choices.feedback: More servers behind the same link do not help once that link is full, and they cost money during the attack.

choices.label: Accept only the CDN’s address ranges, then move the origin
choices.feedback: Right: with the origin closed to everyone but the edge, direct floods are dropped upstream, and a new address the attackers do not know ends the bypass.

choices.label: Lower the DNS TTL on the site’s main record
choices.feedback: The attackers already have the origin’s address; DNS changes do not stop traffic aimed straight at it.

interactive.reveal: An origin behind an edge should accept traffic only from that edge, ideally through a private connection or firewall rules at the network level, and its address should not leak through old DNS records, mail headers or certificates. Then volumetric attacks land on the edge, which has the capacity to absorb them.

seeAlso.why: Rate limiting algorithms behind per-client limits for request floods
CDN edges absorb floods and hide the origin
Autoscaling helps briefly with request floods but needs limits

title: Nagle’s Algorithm and Delayed ACKs
objectives: Explain what Nagle’s algorithm and delayed ACKs each save
Diagnose the stall when a sender writes a request in two pieces
Choose between combining writes and disabling Nagle

cards.title: Two good ideas that collide
cards.body: Nagle’s algorithm (RFC 896) stops a sender from flooding the network with tiny packets: while any sent data is unacknowledged, small writes are held until an ACK arrives or a full segment builds up. A delayed ACK (RFC 1122) lets a receiver wait briefly, hoping to carry the ACK on its own reply; it must still ACK at least every second full-sized segment and within 500 ms. Each saves packets. Together they can deadlock briefly.

cards.title: Worked example: the 40 ms stall in write-write-read
cards.body: A client sends a request as a header write followed by a body write, then waits for the reply.
steps: The header (200 bytes) goes out at once, since nothing is unacknowledged
The body (300 bytes) is held by Nagle, because the header is not yet ACKed
The server cannot reply without the body, so it has nothing to carry an ACK and delays it
The delayed-ACK timer fires: 40 ms is a common Linux minimum, and some systems wait 200 ms
The ACK frees the body, the server replies, and the request finishes about 40 ms late
cards.note: Result. In a data centre with a 0.5 ms round trip, a call that should take about 1 ms takes about 41 ms, roughly 40 times slower, and the delay does not depend on payload size.

cards.title: Fix the write pattern first
cards.body: The cleanest fix is to send each message in one write: build the header and body in one buffer, or use a gather write that hands the kernel several buffers at once. Request and response protocols, such as most RPC and database clients, also set TCP_NODELAY to turn Nagle off, since they care about latency per message. With Nagle off, many tiny writes do become many tiny packets, so buffer in the application.

cards.title: Misconception: delayed ACKs are the bug
cards.body: Each feature helps on its own: delayed ACKs roughly halve ACK traffic on bulk transfers, and Nagle protects slow links from one-byte packets. The stall comes from the pattern, a sender that waits for an ACK the receiver will not send until it has more data. Remove the pattern with one write per message, or turn Nagle off for that socket; turning off delayed ACKs everywhere costs more and is not portable.

cards.title: Trap: benchmarks that only ever send one write
cards.body: A test that sends each request in a single write never sees the stall, so it passes, while production code with a separate header write is slow. The tell is latency stuck near 40 ms or 200 ms whatever the payload size, and in a packet capture, a gap of exactly that length before the second segment. Test with the real client library and the real message pattern.

questions.prompt: What does Nagle’s algorithm do?

choices.label: Delays ACKs so they can ride on replies
Splits large writes into MSS-sized segments
Holds small writes while sent data is unACKed
Resends lost segments sooner than the timer

questions.explanation: Nagle batches small writes on the sender. Delaying ACKs is the receiver-side feature; splitting into segments happens anyway; and early resends are fast retransmit, a different mechanism.

questions.prompt: Why does a receiver delay its ACKs?

choices.label: To send fewer ACKs, often carried on its reply
To slow down a sender that is too fast
To wait for the sender to send its FIN
To give the congestion window time to grow

questions.explanation: Combining the ACK with a reply saves packets. Slowing a sender is the receive window’s job; the FIN is unrelated; and the sender’s window grows on ACKs, so delaying them slows growth.

questions.prompt: Requests inside a data centre (0.5 ms round trip) take a flat 40 ms. The client writes the header and the body separately. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The server’s thread pool is too small
Nagle holds the body while the server delays its ACK
Each request sets up a new TLS session
The switches in the path add 40 ms of queueing delay

questions.explanation: A flat delay matching the delayed-ACK timer, with split writes, is the classic sign. A small thread pool gives delays that grow with load; a TLS setup costs round trips, about 1 ms here; and switch queueing is microseconds to a few ms.

questions.prompt: Which fix removes the stall without filling the network with tiny packets?

choices.label: Turn off delayed ACKs on every server
Set TCP_NODELAY and keep writing byte by byte
Increase the receive window on the server
Send the header and body in one write

questions.explanation: One write per message gives Nagle nothing to hold. Disabling delayed ACKs everywhere is costly and not portable; TCP_NODELAY with byte-sized writes sends a packet per byte; and the window is not the limit.

questions.prompt: Which workload actually benefits from Nagle’s algorithm?

choices.label: An RPC service exchanging small requests and replies
A multiplayer game sending a position update every 16 ms
A remote terminal over a slow link, one key per write
A database client sending short queries

questions.explanation: Batching keystrokes saves many 41-byte packets on a slow link. RPC calls, game updates and database queries are latency-sensitive messages that should go out at once, which is why their clients usually set TCP_NODELAY.

questions.prompt: Order the events in the write-write-read stall.

items.label: The server delays its ACK while waiting for the body
The client sends the header immediately
The body goes out and the server replies
Nagle holds the body until the header is ACKed
The delayed-ACK timer fires and the ACK is sent

questions.explanation: Each side waits for the other until the receiver’s timer breaks the tie.

questions.prompt: A 1-byte keystroke goes in its own IPv4 packet with a 20-byte IP header and a 20-byte TCP header. What percentage of the bytes is payload?
assumptions: No TCP options
Link-layer framing ignored
questions.explanation: Sanity check: about 98% of such a packet is header, which is the waste Nagle was designed to cut on slow links.

flashcards.back: Hold small writes while sent data is unacknowledged.
The receiver waits briefly to carry its ACK on a reply; at least every second full segment, under 500 ms.
One write per message, or TCP_NODELAY on latency-sensitive sockets.

sources.title: RFC 896: Congestion Control in IP/TCP Internetworks
RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts, section 4.2.3.2

mechanism.title: How two packet savers create a pause
steps: A TCP sender can send data as soon as the application writes it. On a slow, shared link in the 1980s, terminals sending one keystroke per packet spent about 40 bytes of headers on every byte typed. John Nagle’s rule, RFC 896, fixed that: if any data is in flight and unacknowledged, hold new small writes and send them together when the ACK arrives or a full segment is ready.

Receivers made a matching optimisation. Instead of acknowledging every segment at once, a receiver may wait a short time, because the application will often reply and the ACK can ride on that reply for free. RFC 1122 bounds the wait at 500 ms and requires an ACK for at least every second full-sized segment, so bulk transfers are acknowledged promptly.

The two collide when a sender writes a message in two parts and then waits for a reply. The first part goes out immediately. The second is small and data is unacknowledged, so Nagle holds it. The receiver has only part of the message, so it has no reply to send and delays its ACK. Neither side moves until the receiver’s delayed-ACK timer fires.

The timer length sets the penalty. Linux commonly uses a minimum of 40 ms, adjusting with observed round trips; other systems have used 200 ms. In a data centre with sub-millisecond round trips, the timer is many times longer than the request itself, so a service can be dozens of times slower than it should be with no sign of load.

There are two clean fixes. Write each message in a single call so there is never a held second part, which also saves system calls. Or set TCP_NODELAY on the socket so small writes go out at once, which most request and response libraries do; then the application should batch its own writes to avoid sending many tiny packets.

useWhen: Diagnosing latency stuck near 40 ms or 200 ms for small requests.
Choosing socket options for RPC, database or game protocols.
avoidWhen: Avoid turning off delayed ACKs system-wide as the fix.
Avoid TCP_NODELAY combined with many tiny writes per message.

rows: Nagle on, one write per message

numbers.title: The price of a split write
assumptions: Round-trip time 0.5 ms, server work 0.5 ms
Delayed-ACK timer 40 ms
Client writes header and body separately
steps: Expected latency with one write: 0.5 ms RTT + 0.5 ms work = 1 ms.
With a split write the body waits for the delayed ACK: + 40 ms.
Actual latency ≈ 41 ms, about 41 times the expected 1 ms.
A client doing 100 such calls one after another spends 4.1 s instead of 0.1 s.
numbers.result: A pattern bug, not load, multiplies latency forty-fold; one write per message removes it.

india.title: Nagle and delayed ACKs in the RFCs and the Linux manual
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 896, written by John Nagle in 1984, describes the small-packet problem and the rule of holding new data while earlier data is unacknowledged. RFC 1122 section 4.2.3.2 lets hosts delay ACKs, but requires an ACK for at least every second full-sized segment and a delay under 0.5 seconds. The Linux tcp(7) manual page documents TCP_NODELAY, which disables Nagle on a socket, and TCP_QUICKACK, which only temporarily leaves delayed-ACK mode.

pitfalls.say: “A flat 40 ms with split writes is Nagle meeting a delayed ACK; I’d send one write per message.”
“The pattern is the problem; one write per message or TCP_NODELAY on that socket fixes it without changing every host.”

takeaways: Nagle holds small writes while data is unacknowledged; delayed ACKs wait to ride on replies.
Write-write-read stalls until the delayed-ACK timer, often 40 ms or 200 ms.
Send each message in one write, or set TCP_NODELAY and buffer in the app.
Latency flat near the ACK timer regardless of size is the tell.

interactive.title: Guess the latency
interactive.prompt: A client in the same data centre as its server (0.5 ms round trip) sends each request as two writes, a header then a body, and waits for the reply. Nagle is on, and the server delays ACKs with a 40 ms timer. The server needs 0.5 ms per request. What latency do you expect?

choices.label: About 1 ms
choices.feedback: That is the latency with one write per message. Here the body waits for an ACK the server is holding back.

choices.label: About 41 ms
choices.feedback: Right: Nagle holds the body until the header is acknowledged, and the server holds the ACK until its 40 ms timer fires.

choices.label: About 80 ms
choices.feedback: The timer fires once per request: after it the body goes out and the reply follows within about a millisecond.

interactive.reveal: Each side waits on the other until the delayed-ACK timer breaks the tie, so the request costs the timer plus the normal 1 ms. Combine the writes or set TCP_NODELAY, and latency drops back to about 1 ms.
